title: Wish it as it comes
hookLine: don't demand that things happen as you wish, but wish them as they happen (Enchiridion 8)

lines: WHICH WAY DOES THE WISH POINT?
cards: You planned a picnic. It rains. You can spend the afternoon at the window, arguing with the sky, replaying the forecast that said ten percent.
Or you can spread the blanket on the living room floor and eat the sandwiches there, listening to the rain on the roof. Same rain either way.
The difference is which way your wishing points: toward the day you wanted, or toward the day that came. Section eight of the handbook flips the usual arrow of wishing around.

teach.h: SEEK NOT THAT THINGS HAPPEN AS YOU WISH.
teach.b: In George Long's translation: "Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life."
The usual order is to wish first and then wait to see if the world agrees. Epictetus says let the world go first, then wish for what came.
It sounds like a trick, and in a way it is: a way of making sure your wishes and the world never fight. The prize he names is a smooth flow; the Greek verb pictures a stream running without snags.
A later Christian writer, Hippolytus, reports that the early Stoics Zeno and Chrysippus compared us to a dog tied to a cart. If the dog wants to follow, it walks along, both pulled and willing.
If it doesn't, it's dragged anyway. The cart goes either way; the only choice is whether to trot or be dragged.
What it doesn't mean: this isn't Epictetus telling anyone to welcome cruelty or stop working for change. The handbook already sorted things into two piles.

Your choices, your effort, your voice are yours, and you use them fully. What it asks is that once something has actually happened, the rain, the canceled flight, the result, you stop demanding it be otherwise.
Centuries later the philosopher Nietzsche put a cousin of this idea into two Latin words: amor fati, love of fate. Epictetus' version is plainer. Not love, necessarily.

how: People who practice Stoicism often try to accept what has already happened as it is, while still putting full effort into what is up to them next.

o: a Latin wish for good luck in what lies ahead
love of fate: wishing for what actually happens
giving up, since you can't change anything at all

games.q: wish it as it comes — tap the pairs.
p: the dog tied to a cart

s: section eight tells you to stop working for change
your effort is yours; it asks you to stop demanding that what already happened be otherwise.
the image of a dog tied to a cart is reported from the early Stoics Zeno and Chrysippus
Hippolytus, a later Christian writer, preserves it.
Epictetus promises you'll get what you want if you wish hard enough
he says to wish for what happens, and you'll have a smooth flow.

games.q: you're the dog tied to the cart, and the cart starts moving. what do you do?
o: dig in your paws and refuse.
games.why: in the Stoic image the cart goes either way; the dog can follow willingly, or be dragged.

practice: Listen for a moment to whatever is happening around you, a car, a fan, a voice in the next room, maybe silence, and let each sound arrive without wishing it different.
Then bring to mind one small surprise from today that you didn't plan, a delay, a message, a change of weather, and turn toward it the same way: as it comes.

wordCard.voice: Amor fati, love of fate: don't ask things to happen as you wish; wish them as they happen, and life flows. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a good flow, life running smoothly; Enchiridion 8 uses the verb form.

carryVoice: Your line: as it comes. The rain falls either way; the wish can point toward it. Day three hundred forty, done.
